speaker_role: independent counselor / former admissions officer panel (Renee Minnik, former senior associate director of admission at Rochester Institute of Technology, 32 years in admissions; Jen Fulbury, former associate director of admission at University of Toledo and former high school counselor; Pete Peekaro, SAT/ACT tutor and former high school teacher - all now consultants at Educational Connections)
commercial_incentive: Yes - panel works for a paid college consulting/test-prep firm (Educational Connections) and promotes scheduling consultations throughout
key_insights: ACT's optional writing section is described as essentially never required by any college the panelists have encountered, so panelists recommend skipping it

For undecided students, panelists note some colleges have shortened or eliminated two-year 'undecided' tracks because those students graduated late, hurting the school's 4-year graduation rate stats; some schools now offer directional 'undecided-in-a-field' tracks instead

Students who enroll in an alternate/backup major (e.g., not their first-choice limited-enrollment program) are advised to plan on graduating in that major, since internal transfer into competitive programs (nursing, PA, architecture) has very limited spots and high competition from both internal and external applicants

For students needing executive-function/learning support, advice is to evaluate classroom size (not just overall school size), since a large school can still have small classes and a strong support structure

Panelists recommend building a genuinely balanced college list (reach/match/likely) as the primary tool for reducing decision-day anxiety, and having candid conversations with students about realistic odds well before senior year rather than after a rejection

No single SAT/ACT target score is meaningful in isolation; panelists recommend taking the test once to have a data point, then comparing to each specific target school's own published middle-50% range, since ranges vary widely by school and even by program within a school

Course rigor and grade trends are described as the 'foundation' of an application; strong test scores can help offset a weaker transcript (showing academic potential), while strong grades with modest testing show it was 'less necessary' as reinforcement

Caution recommended against over-relying on U.S. News & World Report rankings as a filtering tool, since ranking methodology criteria may not reflect what's actually important for an individual student's fit
specific_numbers_or_facts: Renee Minnik: 32 years total in admissions, including 28 years at RIT
Jen Fulbury: 15 years as a high school counselor before working in college admissions
Pete Peekaro: tutoring the SAT/ACT since 2014 (about 12 years)
notable_or_distinctive: The observation that colleges have shortened undecided/exploratory tracks specifically because of pressure on 4-year graduation-rate statistics is a more institutionally-specific insight than typical generic 'it's okay to be undecided' advice.
reliability_notes: Panelists' credentials (former admissions officers/counselors) lend real authority, but the session is also a lead-generation webinar for their paid consulting firm; answers are frequently framed as 'it depends,' reflecting genuine complexity rather than hard rules, and some numeric estimates (e.g., internal transfer odds) are given qualitatively without hard data.
